title: Marty Cagan / SVPG, Product vs Feature Teams
text:
## Product Teams vs Feature Teams

Marty Cagan distinguishes three types of teams that can look structurally identical yet differ profoundly in empowerment and accountability. A Product Team is a cross functional unit of product, design, and engineering that is focused on and measured by outcomes rather than output. Its purpose is to solve problems in ways customers love, yet that work for the business. A Feature Team looks similar but exists to serve the business by delivering prioritized features and projects from a roadmap; it lacks true empowerment. The most common variant is the Delivery Team, essentially an engineering team with a backlog administrator product owner focused on output, not innovation.

## The Four Risks

Product managers on empowered product teams are responsible for addressing four risks before building. Value risk asks whether customers will use or buy it. Usability risk asks whether users can figure out how to use it. Feasibility risk asks whether engineering can build it with the time, skills, and technology available. Business viability risk asks whether the solution works for the various dimensions of the business (sales, marketing, finance, legal). On feature teams, the stakeholders requesting the features assume responsibility for value and viability, which is why those teams are not truly accountable for results.

## Role Implications and Missionaries vs Mercenaries

Empowered product managers require deep knowledge of the customer, the data, the industry, and especially the business. On feature teams the product manager typically functions as a project manager and a partly (unskilled) designer. Cagan frames the cultural difference as teams of missionaries versus teams of mercenaries: missionaries are true believers in the mission who are given problems to solve and the latitude to solve them, while mercenaries build whatever they are told. The essential philosophical difference is outcomes versus output: product teams pursue measurable business outcomes; feature teams deliver a predetermined list of features.

title: Teresa Torres / Product Talk, Opportunity Solution Tree
text:
## The Opportunity Solution Tree

Teresa Torres defines an opportunity solution tree as a simple way of visually representing the paths you might take to reach a desired outcome. It helps product teams stay aligned during continuous discovery while managing the tension between business and customer needs. The tree has four hierarchical levels.

## The Four Levels

The Desired Outcome sits at the root: the business need at the top, typically a product outcome that measures customer behavior or sentiment and is within the team's control. The Opportunity Space is the second level: unmet customer needs, pain points, and desires that, when addressed, drive the desired outcome. Opportunities emerge from story based customer interviews, not from asking customers what they want. Solutions form the third level: the products, features, services, or workflows offered to address opportunities; teams should explore multiple solutions per opportunity rather than committing to the first idea. Assumption Tests form the fourth level: experiments that validate which solutions best create customer value while driving business value.

## Key Principles

The framework rests on a clear distinction between an opportunity (an underlying need) and a solution (a way to address it). A useful test for whether something is truly an opportunity is to ask, is there more than one way to address this. Continuous discovery is built in: teams conduct story based customer interviews continuously and revise the opportunity space every three to four interviews to stay responsive. The outcome emphasizes business viability because, as Torres puts it, when we create business value, we earn the right to serve our customer over time.

## The Problem It Solves

The tree resolves the tension between business and customer needs, unlocks better decisions by letting teams compare and contrast multiple solutions against the same opportunity, and prevents teams from overreacting to isolated pieces of customer feedback by placing each within a structured map of the opportunity space.

title: Intercom (Sean McBride), RICE: Simple prioritization for product managers
text:
## The RICE Scoring Model

Intercom created the RICE scoring model to evaluate and prioritize ideas with more discipline than intuition alone, addressing two common problems: personal bias toward pet ideas, and the difficulty of consistently comparing very different projects. RICE scores each initiative on four factors: Reach, Impact, Confidence, and Effort.

## Reach

Reach estimates how many people each project will affect within a given time period, measured in a concrete unit such as customers per quarter or transactions per month. Use real measurements from product metrics where possible rather than made up numbers.

## Impact

Impact measures how much the project will affect each individual person. Because precise impact is hard to know, Intercom uses a five point multiple choice scale: 3 for massive impact, 2 for high, 1 for medium, 0.5 for low, and 0.25 for minimal. This keeps impact from dominating the score with false precision.

## Confidence

Confidence captures how sure you are of your estimates, expressed as a percentage that acts as a check on projects with lots of supporting data versus those that are more speculative. 100% is high confidence, 80% is medium, 50% is low, and anything below 50% is a total moonshot that probably should not be a priority.

## Effort

Effort estimates the total amount of time a project will require from all members of the team (product, design, engineering), measured in person months, the work one team member does in a month. Effort is counted as a positive whole number (or 0.5 for anything under a month), because unlike the other factors more effort is worse.

## The Formula

The RICE score is (Reach times Impact times Confidence) divided by Effort. The result represents total impact per time worked, letting teams rank projects on a common measure. Reach, Impact, and Confidence are multiplied together and then divided by the Effort so that the score rewards high value work that takes less time.

title: Marty Cagan / SVPG, Product Discovery
text:
## Discovery versus Delivery

Marty Cagan separates product work into two distinct activities. Product discovery is the creative, uncertain phase where the team validates both the market opportunity and the product solution. Delivery is the engineering execution that builds, tests, and ships a production quality product. The central rule is that delivery should only begin once a viable solution has been proven in discovery, so that expensive engineering effort is not spent building the wrong thing.

## The Purpose of Discovery

The purpose of discovery is to discover whether there are real users out there who want this product, and to discover a product solution to the problem that is valuable, usable, and feasible. Instead of using an expensive engineering team to build a polished but untested product over months, discovery uses lightweight prototypes and user testing to validate assumptions rapidly and cheaply. The goal is to tackle the biggest risks first, and to answer the hard questions before committing to building.

## The Pace and Nature of Experimentation

Discovery embraces unpredictability. Cagan describes the product invention process as fundamentally a creative process, more art than science, so it cannot be scheduled like a construction project. Teams iterate quickly on prototypes, run many small experiments, and adjust course continuously based on user feedback rather than following a fixed plan.

## Contrast with the Roadmap and Requirements Approach

Traditional sequential planning treats requirements and design as predictable, scheduled phases and then hands them to engineering to build. Cagan argues this creates waste, because companies commit full engineering teams across multiple release cycles to solutions that were never validated. Discovery inverts the sequence: prototype and test cheaply first, then invest in engineering only after the solution is confirmed to be worth building.

title: Amplitude, The North Star Metric and North Star Framework
text:
## What a North Star Metric Is

Amplitude defines a North Star Metric as the single measure of success for a product team that defines the relationship between the customer problems the product solves and the revenue the company aims to generate. A strong North Star has two parts: a statement of the product vision, and a metric that measures the current product strategy.

## Three Criteria of a Good North Star

First, it aligns to customer value: it captures realized value to the customer by identifying actions inside the product that demonstrate real benefit. Amplitude warns that vanity metrics like Daily Active Users or Registered Users fail as North Stars because they do not reflect what customers actually value. Second, it represents product strategy: someone reading the North Star should understand the company's strategic direction, so the metric must be distinctive to the business model. Third, it is a leading indicator of success: it should predict future revenue rather than report the past. Lagging indicators like monthly revenue tell you what happened rather than predicting what will happen, so the ideal North Star sits as far upstream of revenue as possible.

## The Three Games

Amplitude categorizes products into three engagement models, and the North Star should match the game you are playing. The Attention game is measured by time spent in the product. The Transaction game is measured by transaction volume. The Productivity game is measured by work efficiency and tasks completed. Example North Stars include a Facebook style attention metric such as number of users adding seven friends in the first ten days, a subscription SaaS transaction metric such as trial accounts with more than three users active in week one, and an eCommerce metric such as number of mobile orders delivered.

## The North Star Framework and Input Metrics

The North Star Framework uses a tree in which the North Star Metric is driven by three to five influential, complementary factors called inputs: metrics the team can directly influence that move the main metric forward. Inputs typically address breadth, depth, frequency, and efficiency. Choosing a good North Star delivers better alignment, clearer prioritization, and less wasted work, because it holds product teams accountable for an outcome rather than for shipping velocity alone.

title: Rahul Vohra / First Round Review, How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product Market Fit
text:
## The Sean Ellis Test and the 40% Benchmark

Rahul Vohra built a repeatable engine for product market fit around a leading indicator invented by Sean Ellis: ask users how they would feel if they could no longer use the product, and measure the percentage who answer very disappointed. Ellis found that 40% is the magic threshold. Companies that struggled to grow almost always sat below 40% very disappointed, while companies with strong traction sat above it. Superhuman started at just 22%.

## The Survey

Vohra runs a four question survey, sent only to engaged users who have used the product at least twice in the last two weeks. The questions are: how would you feel if you could no longer use Superhuman (very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, not disappointed); what type of people do you think would most benefit from Superhuman; what is the main benefit you receive from Superhuman; and how can we improve Superhuman for you.

## The Four Step Engine

First, segment by High Expectation Customers, the very disappointed users, and build a detailed persona from them. Superhuman's HXC was Nicole, a busy professional processing 100 to 200 emails a day who values responsiveness and productivity. Focusing on this segment alone lifted the score from 22% to 33%. Second, analyze feedback by disappointment level: study what the very disappointed users love, look at what holds back the somewhat disappointed users but only when your core benefit already resonates with them, and disregard the feedback of the not disappointed. Third, build a balanced roadmap that splits effort roughly 50/50 between doubling down on what users already love and removing the barriers that hold back the on the fence users. Fourth, repeat and measure the very disappointed percentage continuously, weekly, monthly, and quarterly, as the primary metric. Superhuman reached 58% within three quarters.

title: Christensen Institute, Jobs to Be Done Theory
text:
## The Core Idea

Jobs to Be Done is a theory of causation for why customers buy. It reveals the circumstances, or forces, that drive people and organizations toward and away from decisions. Rather than relying on demographics or product features, it exposes the functional, social, and emotional dimensions behind a choice. The central principle is that people do not simply buy or pick products and services; they pull them into their lives to make progress. Everyone has Jobs to Be Done: progress they are trying to make within a particular circumstance.

## Hiring and Firing Products

In the theory's metaphor, people hire products or services when a specific need arises, much as they would employ a contractor or a lawyer, and they fire them when the products no longer do the job well. When circumstances change, people hire different solutions. This reframes competition around the job rather than the product category.

## Three Dimensions of a Job

Every job has three dimensions. The functional dimension covers practical needs such as space, size, or efficiency. The social dimension covers how the choice is perceived by others. The emotional dimension covers psychological aspects such as relieving anxiety or feeling a sense of achievement. A full understanding of a job accounts for all three.

## The Milkshake Example

A fast food restaurant discovered that customers hired its milkshakes for very different jobs throughout the day. On the morning commute the shake was hired to relieve hunger, provide something to do during a long boring drive, and be easy to consume one handed in the car, so its real competition was bagels, bananas, and coffee, not other milkshakes. In the afternoon parents hired the same shake as a treat for their children, a completely different job. Segmenting the milkshake by customer demographics would have hidden these jobs entirely.

## Why This Beats Demographics

The approach differs fundamentally from standard market research that segments by customer attributes and asks why customers buy, which usually yields surface level answers about preferences. Correlations between customer characteristics and purchases do not reveal the underlying circumstance that causes someone to hire a product, and building against those correlations leads to hit or miss innovation.

title: Google re:Work, Set goals with OKRs
text:
## What OKRs Are

Google re:Work describes Objectives and Key Results as a goal setting methodology. Objectives are ambitious and may feel somewhat uncomfortable, describing what you want to achieve. Key Results are measurable and should be easy to grade with a number; they describe how you will know you got there.

## Scoring

Google grades key results on a 0.0 to 1.0 scale, where 1.0 means full achievement. The sweet spot for an OKR grade is 60% to 70%, meaning about 0.6 to 0.7. Consistently scoring 1.0 is a signal that the objectives were not ambitious enough. Grading is meant to be quick and roughly objective, not a precise science.

## Stretch Goals and Sandbagging

Google deliberately sets objectives just beyond the threshold of what seems possible, so hitting 70% is treated as success and hitting 100% is extraordinary performance. The opposite failure is sandbagging: setting easy objectives and meeting them all without fully using available resources, which signals hoarded capacity or insufficient challenge.

## Separation from Performance Reviews

A fundamental principle is that OKRs are not synonymous with employee evaluations. They summarize the work accomplished and the contribution to the organization, but they do not comprehensively assess an individual's performance, because tying stretch goals to compensation drives people to sandbag.

## Best Practices

Set roughly three to five objectives per cycle and about three key results per objective. Key results must describe outcomes, not activities: publish satisfaction levels rather than assess satisfaction. Make OKRs publicly visible across the organization so teams can align. Avoid business as usual objectives and use action oriented language such as ship feature Y or reduce latency to X.

title: John Cutler, 12 Signs You're Working in a Feature Factory (ANTI-PATTERN)
text:
## The Feature Factory Anti-Pattern

John Cutler coined feature factory after a developer friend complained he was just sitting in the factory cranking out features and sending them down the line. A feature factory is an organization that measures itself by output (features shipped) rather than by outcomes (problems solved for customers and the business). Cutler lists twelve warning signs a product person should recognize cold.

## The Twelve Signs

First, no measurement: teams do not measure the impact of their work, or measurement is done in isolation by product management and selectively shared. Second, rapid shuffling of teams and priorities, chronic multitasking and over utilization instead of stable teams with a mission. Third, success theater: celebrating shipping and big launches rather than discussing actual impact. Fourth, infrequent failures and no removed features: the primary measure of success is delivered features, not delivered outcomes, so almost nothing is ever killed. Fifth, no connection to core metrics: teams cannot link their work to business results or customer satisfaction. Sixth, no product manager retrospectives on decision quality: PMs never revisit whether a bet actually paid off. Seventh, obsessing about prioritizing what to build while doing little to validate whether it worked. Eighth, no tweaking: teams move immediately to the next project without iterating on what they just shipped. Ninth, a culture of hand offs, with research, design, build, and post launch support disconnected. Tenth, large batches: features are delivered in big chunks rather than incrementally. Eleventh, chasing upfront revenue by building features to close individual deals with weak economic justification. Twelfth, shiny objects and low visibility for refactoring and debt work, so only new features get attention.

## Why It Matters

The deeper problem is that a feature factory optimizes for the visible and countable (shipping) and starves the invisible but valuable (learning, iteration, killing bad bets, paying down debt). Escaping it means connecting every initiative to a measurable outcome, running discovery, iterating after launch, and being willing to remove features that do not work.

title: Janna Bastow / ProdPad, Why I Invented the Now-Next-Later Roadmap
text:
## The Now-Next-Later Roadmap

Janna Bastow, co founder of ProdPad, invented the Now-Next-Later roadmap in 2012 as an alternative to timeline and Gantt style roadmaps that make date based promises product teams cannot keep. It organizes work by horizons of confidence instead of fixed dates, built on the insight that the further away something is, the more uncertain it is, so the roadmap should reflect that honestly.

## The Three Horizons

Now contains the initiatives the team is actively building. They are clearly defined, detailed, and fully specced, because the team has high confidence about immediate work. Next holds initiatives expected after the current work completes; they carry fewer specifics and details because they are not immediately in view and may depend on what is learned in Now. Later preserves the big boulder blocks: future problems worth solving that do not yet need specification, keeping the product vision alive while leaving room for strategic flexibility.

## Roadmap as a Prototype for Strategy

Bastow frames the roadmap as a prototype for strategy, organized around problems and outcomes rather than features with dates. Her test for a good roadmap: if you can put it in front of anyone and defend every choice without reaching for a date you will have to walk back, you are doing it right. The Now-Next-Later roadmap pairs naturally with OKRs, where the objectives carry the commitment while the roadmap stays flexible. The purpose is to keep teams focused on product discovery, staying aware of customer needs and business opportunities, rather than executing an outdated plan just because it was written down.

title: Jeff Patton, The New Backlog (User Story Mapping)
text:
## The Problem with a Flat Backlog

Jeff Patton argues that arranging user stories in a single prioritized build order creates what he calls a bag of context free mulch. A flat backlog fails to explain what the system does as a whole, fails to ensure complete feature coverage, and makes release planning hard, because you cannot see how the individual stories fit together into a usable product.

## The Story Map Structure

A story map arranges stories in a two dimensional grid rather than a list. The horizontal axis, read left to right, follows the narrative flow of user activities in the order you would explain the behavior of the system. Patton says the order you would tell the story in is the correct order. The vertical axis, read top to bottom, ranks stories by priority: the most essential stories sit at the top and less essential supporting stories hang below.

## Backbone and Walking Skeleton

The backbone is the set of core activities users perform, the high level steps in the narrative such as managing email. The walking skeleton is the minimal system that delivers end to end functionality: all of the backbone plus the highest priority supporting stories under each step. Patton advocates building the walking skeleton first, so you always have something that works across the whole journey.

## Slicing Releases

To plan releases, draw horizontal swim lanes across the map. Each slice cuts through the whole backbone and pulls the highest priority stories from every activity, so a release is always a coherent end to end experience rather than a pile of unrelated features. This prevents the common failure of shipping some parts fully while critical steps (the brakes on the car) get deferred. Story maps act as persistent information radiators that keep the big picture visible throughout development, not artifacts thrown away after planning.

title: Eric Ries, The Lean Startup Principles
text:
## Definition of a Startup

Eric Ries defines a startup as a human institution designed to create a new product or service under conditions of extreme uncertainty. This definition deliberately excludes industry, sector, and company size, so the method applies inside large companies as much as in garages.

## Validated Learning

The core unit of progress for a lean startup is validated learning: a rigorous method for demonstrating progress when embedded in the soil of extreme uncertainty. Instead of waiting to launch a perfect product, entrepreneurs test their fundamental assumptions scientifically through experiments to verify what customers actually want, not what they say they want.

## Build-Measure-Learn

The fundamental activity of a startup is the Build-Measure-Learn feedback loop: turn ideas into products, measure how customers respond, and then learn whether to pivot or persevere. The goal is to minimize the total time through this loop, because the faster you learn, the less capital and time you waste.

## Minimum Viable Product

The Minimum Viable Product is the version of a new product that lets a team start the Build-Measure-Learn loop with the least effort and the fastest path to learning. The first step is to identify the core problem and the riskiest assumptions, then build the MVP to begin learning rapidly, rather than investing in extensive development before any customer contact.

## Innovation Accounting and the Pivot

Innovation accounting is a way to measure progress under uncertainty when traditional metrics like gross revenue are not yet meaningful: define the current baseline, tune the engine toward the ideal, and decide whether to pivot or persevere. A pivot is a structured course correction designed to test a new fundamental hypothesis about the product, strategy, or engine of growth. The five principles of the method are: entrepreneurs are everywhere, entrepreneurship is management, validated learning, innovation accounting, and Build-Measure-Learn.

title: Daniel Zacarias / Folding Burritos, The Complete Guide to the Kano Model
text:
## The Kano Model

The Kano Model, developed by Professor Noriaki Kano, categorizes product features by how they affect customer satisfaction, so teams can prioritize the features that matter most. It plots customer satisfaction (vertical axis, from dissatisfaction to delight) against functionality or investment (horizontal axis, from a feature being absent to fully implemented).

## The Feature Categories

Must-be or Basic features are things customers simply expect: having them does not raise satisfaction, but their absence causes strong dissatisfaction. Performance or One-Dimensional features drive satisfaction in proportion to how much of them you deliver, so every increase in functionality leads to increased satisfaction. Attractive features, also called Delighters or Exciters, are unexpected features that cause a positive reaction when present but no dissatisfaction when absent. Indifferent features are ones customers do not care about either way, so investing in them wastes resources. Reverse features are ones some customers actively do not want, where more functionality lowers their satisfaction.

## Decay Over Time

Attractive features do not stay attractive. Through competition and rising expectations, Attractive features turn into Performance features and then into Must-be features as time goes by. The touchscreen smartphone that once delighted becomes a baseline expectation. This means a product must keep finding new delighters, because yesterday's delighter is tomorrow's basic requirement.

## The Kano Survey

To classify a feature, the Kano questionnaire asks a pair of questions. The functional form asks how would you feel if you had this feature, and the dysfunctional form asks how would you feel if you did not have this feature. Respondents choose from I like it, I expect it, I am neutral, I can tolerate it, or I dislike it. Combining the two answers in an evaluation table places the feature into one of the categories, revealing true customer perception rather than a guess.

title: Joshua Arnold / Black Swan Farming, Cost of Delay
text:
## What Cost of Delay Is

Cost of Delay quantifies the economic impact of time on outcomes. Formally it is the partial derivative of the total expected value with respect to time: the money lost per unit of time when delivery of a feature is delayed. Donald Reinertsen calls Cost of Delay the golden key that unlocks many doors, with an astonishing power to transform the mindset of a development organization, because it puts a number on urgency.

## Combining Urgency and Value

Cost of Delay uniquely integrates two dimensions that people struggle to separate: urgency and value. A feature can be very valuable but not urgent, or urgent but not especially valuable; assessing them separately leads to muddled priorities. Forcing them together as a single money per week figure reveals that delivering early often creates far more value than shaving marginal cost.

## CD3 and Weighted Shortest Job First

The practical prioritization rule derived from Cost of Delay is CD3, Cost of Delay Divided by Duration, also known in SAFe as Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF). By dividing a feature's cost of delay by the time it takes to build, teams sequence the work that delivers the highest economic return per unit of effort first. Short high value jobs go before long low value jobs.

## Economics Over Gut Feel

Cost of Delay replaces gut feel prioritization, arbitrary MoSCoW categorization, and HiPPO driven decisions with economically rational choices. When organizations lack visibility into value and urgency, they default to optimizing for cost and dates, which quietly undermines overall system performance. In the Maersk Line case study, a feature stuck 38 weeks in queues was shown to cost over 200,000 dollars per week, nearly 8 million dollars in lost revenue that better economic visibility could have prevented.

title: Design Council, The Double Diamond
text:
## The Double Diamond

The Design Council introduced the Double Diamond in 2004 to codify and popularize a strategic design process. It maps design work as two connected diamonds: the first works on the problem, the second works on the solution. Each diamond opens up (divergent thinking, exploring widely) and then narrows down (convergent thinking, focusing).

## The Four Phases

Discover is the opening of the first diamond: it helps people understand, rather than simply assume, what the problem is, by spending time with the people affected. Define is the closing of the first diamond: the insights from discovery are used to reframe and clearly define the challenge worth solving. Develop is the opening of the second diamond: it encourages people to give different answers to the clearly defined problem, seeking inspiration elsewhere and co designing with a range of people. Deliver is the closing of the second diamond: solutions are tested at small scale, the ones that do not work are rejected, and the promising ones are refined.

## The Two Diamonds and Right Thing vs Right Way

The first diamond is the problem space: diverge to explore the challenge widely, then converge to define it precisely. The second diamond is the solution space: diverge to generate many possible solutions, then converge to test and implement. Together they capture the two halves of good product work, designing the right thing (the first diamond) and designing the thing right (the second diamond). The framework is not an instruction manual but an invitation to get involved, and it later evolved into the Framework for Innovation, recognizing that discovery can loop back and ideas stay iterative. Published under CC BY 4.0.

title: Josh Seiden (Intercom interview), Outcomes Over Output (ANTI-PATTERN: output obsession)
text:
## Outcomes Over Output

Josh Seiden defines an outcome precisely: an outcome is a change in human behavior that drives business results. This narrow definition is deliberately actionable, because it forces teams to name the specific behavior they are trying to create rather than pointing vaguely at revenue or at a feature list.

## The Three Level Model

Drawing on the Kellogg Foundation Logic Model, Seiden separates three things that are commonly conflated. Output is the features and activities you create, the stuff you make. Outcome is how customer behavior changes as a result of that stuff. Impact is the larger business consequence, the top line result. The common mistake is to treat all three as the same, or to measure output and assume the outcome and impact follow automatically.

## The Anti-Pattern

Just shipping features and moving on is a huge problem for product teams. Without an outcome focus, an organization accumulates a rubble of half finished features that were never validated against real customer behavior, and it measures itself by shipping velocity rather than by whether anything actually changed. This is the output over outcome trap: mistaking motion for progress.

## The Magic Questions

To shift from output to outcomes, Seiden asks three questions when developing a feature: what will people be doing differently as a result of this feature; how will you know you have improved the feature; and are people using this feature in the way we expect. Human behavior change becomes the measurable bridge between what teams build and what the business achieves, so it is the right unit to set goals and measure against.

title: Marc Andreessen, The Pmarca Guide to Startups part 4: The only thing that matters
text:
## Product-Market Fit Defined

Marc Andreessen defines product-market fit as being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market. In his framework a startup's life has two phases: before product-market fit (BPMF) and after product-market fit (APMF), and the single most important thing a startup can do is get to product-market fit.

## The Market Is the Dominant Factor

Andreessen argues the market matters more than the team or the product. He cites Rachleff's Law: when a great team meets a lousy market, market wins; when a lousy team meets a great market, market wins. In a great market the market pulls product out of the startup, because customers are actively looking for a solution and will drag a viable product out of you regardless of pedigree. Neither a stellar team nor a fantastic product will redeem a bad market.

## How You Know

You can always feel when product-market fit is not happening: the customers are not quite getting value out of the product, word of mouth is not spreading, usage is not growing fast, press reviews are kind of blah, the sales cycle takes too long, and lots of deals never close. You can also always feel when product-market fit is happening: the customers are buying the product just as fast as you can make it, or usage is growing just as fast as you can add more servers, money from customers is piling up, and you are hiring sales and support staff as fast as you can.

## The Imperative

Andreessen's central recommendation is that when you are before product-market fit, you should focus obsessively on getting to product-market fit, doing whatever is required, including changing out people, rewriting the product, moving into a different market, and telling customers no when you do not want to, and yes when you do not want to, in order to get there. Everything else is secondary.

title: Melissa Perri (Mind the Product talk), Escaping the Build Trap (ANTI-PATTERN)
text:
## The Build Trap Defined

Melissa Perri describes the Build Trap as a state where product teams are defining and shipping software with no measures of success, focusing on delivering features rather than validating their value. Teams get stuck maximizing the amount of things they build and ship, instead of maximizing the value of what they build. It is the organizational version of the output over outcome mistake.

## Why It Happens

The root cause is a flawed mental model in which the company believes feature ideas plus code equals profit. This creates an endless cycle in which product managers feed requirements to developers, who churn out features, without anyone questioning whether customers actually benefit. In reality product development is part of a system of value exchange: the business solves customer problems, and customers reciprocate with money or data or attention. Organizations in the build trap fail to see this dynamic and mistake shipping for value creation.

## Output versus Outcome

The talk contrasts outputs (the features shipped) with outcomes (the customer value actually realized). The build trap prioritizes outputs; escaping it requires focusing on outcomes, that is, whether customer problems are genuinely solved.

## Escaping the Trap

Perri names three controllable factors. Process: agile does not have a brain, so it can tell you how to work together but never what to build. Strategy: real strategy flows from a clear vision and mission and gives teams a framework to navigate the uncertainty of product development, rather than a list of features. Culture: the organization must reward learning and reaching outcomes rather than shipping outputs. The escape is to become a customer centric, product led organization that evaluates its strategy by whether it meets outcomes and lets product teams get close to their customers.

title: Ben Horowitz, Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager
text:
## The CEO of the Product

Ben Horowitz's classic memo frames a good product manager as the CEO of the product. The point is accountability, not authority: a good PM takes full responsibility and measures themselves by the success of the product, but does not command all the functions. They manage strategic outcomes while leaving engineering and other teams autonomy over execution. The modern reading corrects the common misuse of this line, the PM does not boss people around like a real CEO, they own the result.

## What Good PMs Do

Good product managers know the market, the product, the product line, and the competition extremely well, and operate from a strong basis of knowledge and confidence. They take full responsibility and measure themselves by product success. They are the voice of the customer inside the company. They define good products that can be executed with a strong effort, and they manage the product team, focusing it on revenue and customers. They anticipate serious product flaws and create real solutions, and they create leverageable collateral (FAQs, presentations, white papers).

## What Bad PMs Do

Bad product managers make excuses: not enough funding, the engineering manager is an idiot, Microsoft has ten times the engineers, they are overworked, they do not get enough direction. They spend their day putting out fires and answering the same questions again and again. They are gophers for engineering, consumed by meetings and project management minutiae. They gather requirements by consensus and chase whatever features competitors ship, or let engineering build whatever is technically most interesting rather than what customers need.

## Communication

Good product managers communicate crisply to engineering in writing as well as verbally, and they do not give direction informally. They take written positions on hard issues so that their reasoning is on record and can be judged against reality. Bad product managers voice their opinions verbally and then, when their prediction turns out wrong, complain that the powers that be made the bad decision. Putting it in writing is a core discipline of the role.

title: Teresa Torres / Product Talk, What Is Continuous Product Discovery
text:
## Discovery versus Delivery

Teresa Torres defines product discovery as the work a team does to decide what to build, while product delivery is the work the team does to build, ship, and maintain a production quality product. The two run in parallel: discovery is not a phase that ends before delivery begins, it is ongoing.

## Why Continuous

Torres argues that good teams engage with customers at least weekly, because digital products are never finished and customer needs keep shifting. Continuous contact counters the curse of knowledge, the bias in which a team that knows its product too well makes decisions disconnected from customer reality. Rather than a big research phase up front, discovery becomes a steady habit of small, frequent research activities in pursuit of a clear desired outcome.

## The Product Trio

Discovery is led by a product trio: the product manager, a designer, and a software engineer. They should interview customers together and collaborate on and execute assumption tests together, so that the three perspectives (value, usability, feasibility) are all present when decisions are made, instead of handing findings from one function to another.

## The Weekly Activities

Torres names two primary discovery activities. Customer interviewing surfaces opportunities: unmet needs, pain points, and desires. Assumption testing surfaces solutions: small experiments that check whether a proposed solution will work before it is built. The underlying structure is start with an outcome, discover opportunities, then discover solutions, usually visualized with an opportunity solution tree.

title: Amplitude, AARRR Pirate Metrics Framework (Dave McClure)
text:
## AARRR Pirate Metrics

Dave McClure introduced the Pirate Metrics framework in a 2007 talk to bring order to chaotic product growth. The acronym AARRR, which sounds like a pirate's exclamation, names five sequential stages of the customer lifecycle that product teams should measure and optimize.

## The Five Stages

Acquisition identifies the initial user entry points for engaging with the product; metrics include new signups, qualified leads, and customer acquisition cost, and teams optimize channels and messaging to reach high volume, low cost audiences. Activation measures how effectively users move from initial curiosity to understanding the value the product provides; metrics include activation rate, time to activate, and free to paid conversion, and success is marked by users hitting their aha moment. Retention shows stickiness by measuring how many users return over time; retention rate, churn rate, and customer lifetime value reveal whether users find lasting value. Referral gauges how many users become net promoters or evangelists who tell others, tracked through invite shares and recipient conversion; referrals produce organic growth at minimal cost. Revenue demonstrates how well the company turns engaged users into paying customers, through metrics like monthly recurring revenue, net revenue retention, and average revenue per user.

## Why It Exists

McClure designed the framework to combat vanity metrics and superficial measurements such as raw likes or pageviews. Rather than celebrating aesthetically pleasing graphs, teams should focus on the few numbers that matter, the metrics that genuinely indicate sustainable, profitable growth. A common modern critique reorders the stages as RARRA, arguing that for many products retention should come first because acquiring users who never come back is wasted spend.

title: Brian Balfour, Growth Loops are the New Funnels
text:
## Why Funnels Fall Short

Brian Balfour, with Casey Winters, Kevin Kwok, and Andrew Chen, argues that the AARRR funnel, while a good starting point, does not represent how the fastest growing products actually grow. He names three problems with the funnel. Strategic silos: separating product, marketing, and monetization strategy ignores how they interconnect. Functional silos: marketing owns acquisition and product owns retention, so each function optimizes independently and undermines the collective goal. Linear growth constraints: the funnel mindset of put more in at the top to get more out at the bottom demands ever increasing inputs and is unsustainable.

## Growth Loops Defined

A growth loop is a closed system where the inputs, through some process, generate more of an output that can be reinvested into the input. Unlike a funnel's one way trajectory, a loop feeds its own output back to the start, so each cycle can produce more of the next cycle's fuel. This is what enables compounding growth rather than linear growth.

## Why Loops Win

Loops outperform funnels for two reasons. First, compounding mechanics: because each cycle's output reinvests into the input, growth can be exponential rather than linear. Second, integrated systems: a loop combines product, channel, and monetization dynamics into one company specific system that is much harder for competitors to copy than a single channel tactic. Balfour's team identified more than twenty types of loops, serving different goals such as acquiring new users, bringing back returning users, building defensibility, or improving efficiency, illustrated with cases like Pinterest and SurveyMonkey.

title: Lenny Rachitsky / Lenny's Newsletter, How to get into product management (the PM role)
text:
## What a Product Manager Actually Does

Lenny Rachitsky describes the product manager role as marshaling the resources of a team to deliver business impact. Teams are handed problems, for example grow adoption of a product, reduce churn of a service, or increase conversion of a flow, and the PM's job is to guide the team to make it less of a problem. The role is defined by outcomes and problems to solve, not by a fixed feature list.

## Influence Without Authority

A defining feature of the job is that PMs operate through influence without formal authority: they rarely manage the engineers, designers, and others they depend on, so they lead by building trust and keeping everyone aligned on shared objectives. This is why credibility and communication matter so much more than title.

## Execution Is Non-Negotiable

Rachitsky is blunt that execution is the foundational skill: a PM who is good at nothing else but execution is still valuable to a team, while a team with a PM who cannot execute is better off without that PM. Execution here means aligning the roadmap, managing deadlines, hunting for and removing blockers, and keeping the team always moving forward.

## What Strong PMs Have in Common

Effective product managers share a set of traits: follow through, meaning they say what they will do and then do what they say; obsession with solving customer problems rather than shipping features; detail orientation and thorough preparation; decisions grounded in data and clear principles rather than opinion; and excellent communication across many formats, written and verbal. Being both trusting and trustworthy, and knowing the difference between trust and blind faith, underpins the whole role.

title: Agile Business Consortium (DSDM), What is MoSCoW Prioritization
text:
## MoSCoW Prioritization

MoSCoW is a prioritization technique from the DSDM agile framework, maintained by the Agile Business Consortium. The letters stand for Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won't have this time. The capital letters M, S, C, W come from these four categories, and the technique is used to agree which requirements are essential for a given delivery.

## The Four Categories

Must have requirements are the Minimum Usable SubseT (the origin of the word MUST): there is no point delivering on the target date without them, and if they are not delivered there is no point deploying the solution on the intended date. The test is that if a Must have went unmet, the release would be cancelled or has no value. Should have requirements are important but not vital; the solution is still viable without them, but leaving them out causes meaningful business pain, perhaps with a workaround. Could have requirements are wanted or desirable but less important, with less impact if left out than a Should have; they form the primary contingency pool and are delivered only if circumstances allow. Won't have this time requirements are explicitly excluded from the current timeframe; recording them clarifies scope and prevents informal reintroduction later.

## Effort Allocation

DSDM recommends that Must have requirements make up no more than 60% of the total effort, so that there is enough buffer capacity to handle unknowns and manage risk with confidence. Could haves are typically set at around 20% of effort and act as the deliberate contingency buffer that can be dropped when things go wrong without threatening the deadline. A Must have proportion much higher than 60% introduces significant project failure risk unless conditions are exceptionally favorable, with accurate estimates, a well understood approach, an established team, and low external risk.
